evidence_set: The abstract's statement that abstinence ran from 5 days to 3 weeks in most studies refers to the review's studies as a whole (31 identified); the Dopamine transporter results paragraph gives no abstinence durations for the 9 amphetamine-type transporter studies (refs 27–35, which include McCann et al. 1998 and 2008 and Johanson et al. 2006). The main text mentions abstinence for two of the nine only in other contexts: about three months for Johanson et al. (ref 28) in the VMAT2 result, and dopamine receptor density and release still down-regulated after 9 months for Volkow et al. 2015 (ref 35). The authors note marked dopaminergic differences even in studies of several months' abstinence.

The reviewers state that in the majority of the PET studies (Table 2) the methamphetamine groups reported extensive use of other psychoactive drugs while comparison groups reported only limited drug use, which they say makes it extremely difficult to separate methamphetamine-related effects on cognitive functioning from those of other drugs; they add that, despite these caveats, the PET literature tends to describe any brain or cognitive difference as a dysfunction specific to people who use methamphetamine.

evidence_set: SPECT study (Chou et al., 2007) of 5 people with methamphetamine dependence, scanned while their urine was positive for methamphetamine and again after 2 weeks of abstinence, with 7 controls retested after 1 week: striatal transporter availability rose by 5 to 38% (mean 20%) in the methamphetamine group, while controls changed by −14 to +13%; the reviewers note that the groups were not compared statistically in a within-subjects manner (their changes were not tested against each other).

The authors state that the transporter reductions were smaller than those reported in Parkinson's disease (36–71%), but that in three people in the methamphetamine group the transporter level fell within the range seen in low-severity Parkinson's disease. The three are not identified, and neither their values nor that range is given in numbers; individual values appear only as unlabelled points in Figures 2 and 3. The authors suggest these relatively young people probably had no extrapyramidal symptoms because they could still compensate.

evidence_set: For comprehension knowledge only, the group difference depended on risk-of-bias rating (Qbet 7.69, df 1, p=.006): −0.67 SD (95% CI −0.92 to −0.43) in high risk-of-bias studies vs −0.09 SD (95% CI −0.42 to 0.24) in unclear risk-of-bias studies. The seven other domains tested did not differ by rating; reaction and decision speed had too few data points to be tested. The authors note that retained participants who used methamphetamine may have been in better health than those who dropped out or did not take part, so attrition may have somewhat attenuated the group differences.

The reviewers conclude that the preponderance of the data suggests that methamphetamine use causes mild cognitive decline in at least some individuals, likely observable in some but not all; five of their six hypotheses received at least some support (most data did not support the dose-related one), and they argue that because animal studies typically use designs that can support causal inference, that evidence should likely be weighed more heavily than other forms of evidence.

evidence_set: The Methods describe five sensitivity analyses: including week-1 results; imputing missing urine samples as positive (a not-missing-at-random assumption); adjusting for imbalanced baseline characteristics and baseline correlates of missing or positive samples; including late final visits; and stratifying by baseline intensity of use. The text does not say whether these were prespecified; only the primary model is called prespecified. The Results report significant effects favouring mirtazapine with week-1 results included, with missing samples imputed as positive and with baseline correlates controlled for, giving the estimates only in the supplement's eTable (not read). No significant effect was seen when stratifying by intensity of use, and the late-visit analysis is not reported in the text. No evidence of unblinding at week 24: 19 (46%) on mirtazapine and 23 (49%) on placebo guessed their arm correctly (P = .83).
